# Central-reflection retention: three interval fibers and nonheavy sharpness

For any induced mixed convex source with n=d=1 and at most three positive
interval fibers, some actual mixed point retains at least half the mixed
mass under central reflection. The factor one half is sharp even as a
limit of three positive fibers, none individually carrying half the mass.
Binary products give analogous nonheavy sharpness at 2^-n for every n>=1.
No assertion for arbitrary numbers of interval fibers is made here.

## 1. Definitions and the two-endpoint overlap formula

For a mixed point y=(j,t), let

    R(j,t)=mu(C intersect (2y-C) intersect Lambda).

For interval fibers I_z this is exactly

    R(j,t)=sum_z |I_z intersect (2t-I_(2j-z))|,         (1)

with missing or zero-length fibers contributing zero. The reflected
intersection is centrally symmetric about y and is contained in C.
Every closed halfspace through y therefore contains at least half of its
retained mass. Thus a retention bound R(j,t)>=M/2 would imply depth at
least1/4 at that point, but only the stated retention theorem is proved
below.

For intervals A=[A_0,A_0+a], D=[D_0,D_0+c] of lengths a,c>0, put
`s=2t-A_0-D_0`. Their overlap length is

    |A intersect (2t-D)|
       =[min(a,c,s,a+c-s)]_+.                         (2)

This follows directly from
`[min(a,s)-max(0,s-c)]_+`; splitting at the four endpoints proves (2).
The reversed pair has the same overlap length by reflection.

## 2. Exact lower bound for three convex-compatible fibers

Positive integer interval fibers form a consecutive set. After translating
the base, the three-fiber case has A at -1, B at0, and D at1. Write their
lengths as a,b,c. Convex compatibility gives

    (A+D)/2 subset B,

and in particular `b>=(a+c)/2`. Let t be the midpoint of B. If its lower
endpoint is B_0, containment gives

    (A_0+D_0+a+c)/2-b <= B_0 <= (A_0+D_0)/2.

Consequently the scalar s in (2), evaluated at `t=B_0+b/2`, obeys

    a+c-b <= s <= b.                                 (3)

If b<a+c, both s and a+c-s are at least a+c-b. If b>=a+c, the trivial
zero bound suffices. In either case, (2)--(3) yield

    |A intersect (2t-D)|>=min(a,c,(a+c-b)_+).

The middle interval reflects into itself about t, and the two endpoint
contributions agree. Therefore

    R(0,t)>=b+2min(a,c,(a+c-b)_+).                     (4)

At either extreme integer base the midpoint of its own fiber retains its
whole length. Thus the maximum reflection retention has the explicit bound

    R_max>=max{a,c,b+2min(a,c,(a+c-b)_+)}.             (5)

If any of a,b,c is at least M/2, its own midpoint already retains at least
M/2. Otherwise put `x=a+c-b>0`. The other two nonheavy inequalities give
`x<2a` and `x<2c`. Thus `min(a,c,x)>=x/2`, and (4) gives

    R(0,t)>=b+x=a+c>M/2.

This proves the half-mass theorem for three fibers. With one or two positive
fibers, a largest fiber has mass at least M/2 and its midpoint suffices.
Extra zero-length integer fibers, if present, change no H_1 measure or
reflection contribution. The selected centers always lie in actual
positive fibers; no rounding or extension of the source is used.

## 3. Sharpness in the genuinely nonheavy regime

For `0<epsilon<1`, take the actual body with integer fibers

    I_-1=[0,1], I_0=[0,1], I_1=[0,epsilon].

Its lower boundary is zero and its concave upper boundary on [-1,1] is
one on [-1,0] and `1-(1-epsilon)z` on [0,1]. Hence these are exactly its
positive integer fibers. Total mixed mass is `M=2+epsilon`; every fiber
has length strictly less than M/2.

At the middle base, self-overlap is at most one and each endpoint overlap
is at most epsilon. These bounds are simultaneously attained at t=1/2:
the reflection of [0,epsilon] is [1-epsilon,1], contained in [0,1]. Thus

    max_t R(0,t)=1+2epsilon.

At the two extreme bases only their own fibers contribute, with maxima
one and epsilon. Therefore

    R_max/M=(1+2epsilon)/(2+epsilon) ->1/2             (6)

as epsilon decreases to zero. This is an exact maximization, not merely
one selected center's value. Two equal adjacent interval fibers attain
one half exactly; (6) keeps three positive nonheavy fibers throughout.

For any n>=1, multiply this body by `[0,1]^(n-1)` in additional INTEGER
coordinates. The resulting full ambient body has `3*2^(n-1)` positive
interval fibers and total mass `2^(n-1)(2+epsilon)`. Reflection about an
integer point of a binary coordinate retains only the copy at that same
binary coordinate: reflection of the opposite binary value is -1 or2,
outside the projection. Hence its maximal retained mass is still exactly
`1+2epsilon`, and

    R_max/M=(1+2epsilon)/[2^(n-1)(2+epsilon)] ->2^-n.

Every individual fiber has mass at most one, strictly below
`M/2^n=(2+epsilon)/2`. Thus a proposed universal 2^-n retention constant
cannot be improved even by excluding all heavy-fiber cases. The product
calculation supplies sharpness, not a proof of that universal inequality.
